summary:
AstroRing is a health-monitoring system designed to help astronauts keep track of their health during long-duration space missions. By combining a smart ring with monitoring software, astronauts can check their health conditions, recognize possible risks, and take action when needed, especially when communication with Earth is delayed.

The software tracks important health indicators such as heart rate, blood oxygen levels, breathing rate, body temperature, and stress levels. It also considers environmental factors, including radiation exposure, oxygen levels, carbon dioxide, and cabin pressure, which can affect astronauts' health during a mission.

One of the main features of AstroRing is its alert system, which notifies astronauts when unusual changes are detected and suggests possible actions. The software also includes graphs to track health changes over time, sleep monitoring, and tools to evaluate potential health risks.

Another feature is the Heads-Up Display (HUD), which allows astronauts to view their health information through a camera interface without constantly checking a separate screen.

Using research and information from NASA, our team developed a software prototype that simulates different health conditions and emergency situations to demonstrate how the system would work.

Our goal with AstroRing is to make health monitoring easier, more accessible, and more practical for astronauts during future missions to the Moon and Mars.
details:
We created AstroRing to help astronauts better understand their health during long space missions. We researched NASA studies to learn about the health risks astronauts face and used that information to develop our software.

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to build an interactive dashboard with health readings, alerts, graphs, and a camera-based display. We also added different scenarios, such as low oxygen levels, high carbon dioxide, and radiation exposure, to test how our software responds.

When designing AstroRing, we considered comfort, weight, accessibility, and ease of use. We chose a ring because it is small and would not interfere much with astronauts' daily activities.

What makes our project different is that it combines health information with environmental conditions and suggests actions astronauts can take. Our goal is to help astronauts recognize potential health problems earlier and become more independent during future space missions.
dataRefs: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes
